source: Next morning the not-yet-subsided sea rolled in long slow billows of mighty bulk, and striving in the Pequod’s gurgling track, pushed her on like giants’ palms outspread. The strong, unstaggering breeze abounded so, that sky and air seemed vast outbellying sails; the whole world boomed before the wind. Muffled in the full morning light, the invisible sun was only known by the spread intensity of his place; where his bayonet rays moved on in stacks. Emblazonings, as of crowned Babylonian kings and queens, reigned over everything. The sea was as a crucible of molten gold, that bubblingly leaps with light and heat.

Long maintaining an enchanted silence, Ahab stood apart; and every time the tetering ship loweringly pitched down her bowsprit, he turned to eye the bright sun’s rays produced ahead; and when she profoundly settled by the stern, he turned behind, and saw the sun’s rearward place, and how the same yellow rays were blending with his undeviating wake.

“Ha, ha, my ship! thou mightest well be taken now for the sea-chariot of the sun. Ho, ho! all ye nations before my prow, I bring the sun to ye! Yoke on the further billows; hallo! a tandem, I drive the sea!”
But suddenly reined back by some counter thought, he hurried towards the helm, huskily demanding how the ship was heading.
“East-sou-east, sir,” said the frightened steersman.
“Thou liest!” smiting him with his clenched fist. “Heading East at this hour in the morning, and the sun astern?”
Upon this every soul was confounded; for the phenomenon just then observed by Ahab had unaccountably escaped every one else; but its very blinding palpableness must have been the cause.

Thrusting his head half way into the binnacle, Ahab caught one glimpse of the compasses; his uplifted arm slowly fell; for a moment he almost seemed to stagger. Standing behind him Starbuck looked, and lo! the two compasses pointed East, and the Pequod was as infallibly going West.

But ere the first wild alarm could get out abroad among the crew, the old man with a rigid laugh exclaimed, “I have it! It has happened before. Mr. Starbuck, last night’s thunder turned our compasses—that’s all. Thou hast before now heard of such a thing, I take it.”
“Aye; but never before has it happened to me, sir,” said the pale mate, gloomily.

Here, it must needs be said, that accidents like this have in more than one case occurred to ships in violent storms. The magnetic energy, as developed in the mariner’s needle, is, as all know, essentially one with the electricity beheld in heaven; hence it is not to be much marvelled at, that such things should be. Instances where the lightning has actually struck the vessel, so as to smite down some of the spars and rigging, the effect upon the needle has at times been still more fatal; all its loadstone virtue being annihilated, so that the before magnetic steel was of no more use than an old wife’s knitting needle. But in either case, the needle never again, of itself, recovers the original virtue thus marred or lost; and if the binnacle compasses be affected, the same fate reaches all the others that may be in the ship; even were the lowermost one inserted into the kelson.

Deliberately standing before the binnacle, and eyeing the transpointed compasses, the old man, with the sharp of his extended hand, now took the precise bearing of the sun, and satisfied that the needles were exactly inverted, shouted out his orders for the ship’s course to be changed accordingly. The yards were hard up; and once more the Pequod thrust her undaunted bows into the opposing wind, for the supposed fair one had only been juggling her.

Meanwhile, whatever were his own secret thoughts, Starbuck said nothing, but quietly he issued all requisite orders; while Stubb and Flask—who in some small degree seemed then to be sharing his feelings—likewise unmurmuringly acquiesced. As for the men, though some of them lowly rumbled, their fear of Ahab was greater than their fear of Fate. But as ever before, the pagan harpooneers remained almost wholly unimpressed; or if impressed, it was only with a certain magnetism shot into their congenial hearts from inflexible Ahab’s.
For a space the old man walked the deck in rolling reveries. But chancing to slip with his ivory heel, he saw the crushed copper sight-tubes of the quadrant he had the day before dashed to the deck.

“Thou poor, proud heaven-gazer and sun’s pilot! yesterday I wrecked thee, and to-day the compasses would fain have wrecked me. So, so. But Ahab is lord over the level loadstone yet. Mr. Starbuck—a lance without a pole; a top-maul, and the smallest of the sail-maker’s needles. Quick!”

Accessory, perhaps, to the impulse dictating the thing he was now about to do, were certain prudential motives, whose object might have been to revive the spirits of his crew by a stroke of his subtile skill, in a matter so wondrous as that of the inverted compasses. Besides, the old man well knew that to steer by transpointed needles, though clumsily practicable, was not a thing to be passed over by superstitious sailors, without some shudderings and evil portents.

“Men,” said he, steadily turning upon the crew, as the mate handed him the things he had demanded, “my men, the thunder turned old Ahab’s needles; but out of this bit of steel Ahab can make one of his own, that will point as true as any.”
Abashed glances of servile wonder were exchanged by the sailors, as this was said; and with fascinated eyes they awaited whatever magic might follow. But Starbuck looked away.

With a blow from the top-maul Ahab knocked off the steel head of the lance, and then handing to the mate the long iron rod remaining, bade him hold it upright, without its touching the deck. Then, with the maul, after repeatedly smiting the upper end of this iron rod, he placed the blunted needle endwise on the top of it, and less strongly hammered that, several times, the mate still holding the rod as before. Then going through some small strange motions with it—whether indispensable to the magnetizing of the steel, or merely intended to augment the awe of the crew, is uncertain—he called for linen thread; and moving to the binnacle, slipped out the two reversed needles there, and horizontally suspended the sail-needle by its middle, over one of the compass-cards. At first, the steel went round and round, quivering and vibrating at either end; but at last it settled to its place, when Ahab, who had been intently watching for this result, stepped frankly back from the binnacle, and pointing his stretched arm towards it, exclaimed,—“Look ye, for yourselves, if Ahab be not lord of the level loadstone! The sun is East, and that compass swears it!”
One after another they peered in, for nothing but their own eyes could persuade such ignorance as theirs, and one after another they slunk away.
In his fiery eyes of scorn and triumph, you then saw Ahab in all his fatal pride.

paragraphs: The next morning the sea, not yet calmed, rolled in long, slow swells of enormous bulk, and, surging along in the Pequod's gurgling wake, pushed her forward like the outspread palms of giants. The strong, steady breeze blew so abundantly that sky and air seemed like vast billowing sails; the whole world boomed along before the wind. Muffled in the full morning light, the sun could not be seen, and was known only by the spread-out intensity of the place where he stood, where his bayonet rays moved forward in stacks. Heraldic splendors, as of crowned Babylonian kings and queens, reigned over everything. The sea was like a crucible of molten gold, bubbling and leaping with light and heat.

Keeping a spellbound silence for a long time, Ahab stood apart. Every time the teetering ship dipped her bowsprit low, he turned to look at the bright rays of the sun stretching out ahead; and when she sank deep by the stern, he turned around and saw where the sun stood behind them, and how the same yellow rays were blending with his unswerving wake.

But, suddenly pulled up short by some contrary thought, he hurried to the helm and asked hoarsely which way the ship was heading.
"East-southeast, sir," said the frightened steersman.
"You lie!" striking him with his clenched fist. "Heading east at this hour in the morning, and the sun astern?"
At this everyone was dumbfounded; for somehow the phenomenon Ahab had just noticed had escaped everyone else — though its very glaring obviousness must have been the reason.

Standing deliberately in front of the binnacle and eyeing the turned-around compasses, the old man now took the exact bearing of the sun with the edge of his outstretched hand. modern_da.title: Kapitel 124 — Nålen
paragraphs: Næste morgen rullede havet, der endnu ikke var faldet til ro, i lange, langsomme dønninger af enorm vægt, og mens de bølgede frem i Pequods klukkende kølvand, skubbede de hende fremad som kæmpers udbredte håndflader. Den stærke, jævne brise blæste så rigeligt, at himmel og luft lignede enorme, svulmende sejl; hele verden buldrede af sted foran vinden. Solen var indhyllet i det fulde morgenlys og kunne ikke ses; man kendte den kun på den udbredte styrke, hvor den stod, og hvor dens bajonetstråler rykkede frem i stakke. Heraldisk pragt, som af kronede babyloniske konger og dronninger, herskede over alt. Havet var som en digel med smeltet guld, der boblede og sprang af lys og varme.

Ahab stod længe for sig selv i fortryllet tavshed. Hver gang det vuggende skib dykkede med bovsprydet langt ned, vendte han sig for at se på solens klare stråler, der strakte sig frem foran; og når hun sank dybt i agterstavnen, vendte han sig om og så, hvor solen stod bag dem, og hvordan de samme gule stråler smeltede sammen med hans ubøjelige kølvand.

»Ha, ha, mit skib! Man kunne nu godt tage dig for solens havvogn. Ho, ho! Alle I nationer foran min stævn, jeg bringer jer solen! Spænd for på de fjerne bølger; halløj! Som et forspand kører jeg havet!«
Men pludselig blev han standset af en modsat tanke, skyndte sig hen til rattet og spurgte hæst, hvilken vej skibet styrede.
»Øst-sydøst, sir,« sagde den forskrækkede rorgænger.
»Du lyver!« sagde han og slog ham med knyttet næve. »Styrer øst på denne tid af morgenen, og med solen agter?«
Alle stod målløse ved det; for på en eller anden måde var det fænomen, Ahab lige havde lagt mærke til, undsluppet alle andre — selv om netop dets skinnende åbenlyshed må have været grunden.

Ahab stak hovedet halvt ind i nathuset, fik et glimt af kompasserne, og hans løftede arm sank langsomt; et øjeblik så han næsten ud til at vakle. Starbuck stod bag ham og så efter og — se! — de to kompasser pegede mod øst, og Pequod sejlede lige så ufejlbarligt mod vest.

Men før den første vilde forskrækkelse kunne brede sig blandt besætningen, udbrød den gamle mand med en stiv latter: »Jeg har det! Det er sket før. Mr. Starbuck, i nat har tordenen vendt vores kompasser om — det er det hele. Du har vel hørt om sligt før nu.«
»Ja; men det er aldrig sket for mig før, sir,« sagde den blege styrmand dystert.

Her må det siges, at ulykker som denne er sket for mere end ét skib i voldsomme storme. Den magnetiske kraft, som den udvikler sig i sømandens nål, er, som alle ved, i bund og grund ét med den elektricitet, man ser på himlen; så det er ikke meget at undres over, at sligt kan ske. I tilfælde, hvor lynet virkelig har ramt skibet, så noget af rær og rigning er slået ned, har virkningen på nålen til tider været endnu mere skæbnesvanger: al dens magnetiske kraft er blevet ødelagt, så det tidligere magnetiske stål ikke var til mere gavn end en gammel kones strikkepind. Men i begge tilfælde får nålen aldrig selv sin oprindelige kraft tilbage, når den først er forringet eller tabt; og hvis nathusets kompasser er påvirket, rammer den samme skæbne alle de andre, der måtte være i skibet, selv hvis det laveste sad indfældet i kølsvinet, tømmeret der løber langs kølen indvendig i lasten.

Den gamle mand stillede sig i ro foran nathuset og så på de omvendte kompasser og tog nu solens nøjagtige pejling med kanten af sin udstrakte hånd. Da han var sikker på, at nålene var helt omvendt, råbte han ordre om, at skibets kurs skulle ændres, så den passede. Rårne blev brasset hårdt an, og endnu en gang drev Pequod sin uforfærdede stævn ind i den modsatte vind, for den formodede gode vind havde kun narret hende.

Imens sagde Starbuck ingenting, hvad hans egne hemmelige tanker så end var, men gav stille alle de nødvendige ordrer; mens Stubb og Flask — som i en lille grad dengang syntes at dele hans følelser — ligeledes føjede sig uden et mukkeri. Hvad mandskabet angik, rumlede nogle af dem lavt, men deres frygt for Ahab var større end deres frygt for skæbnen. Men som altid før forblev de hedenske harpunerer næsten helt upåvirkede; eller hvis de var påvirket, var det kun af en vis magnetisme, der blev skudt ind i deres beslægtede hjerter fra den ubøjelige Ahabs.

En tid gik den gamle mand rundt på dækket, fortabt i bølgende dagdrømme. Men da han kom til at glide med sin elfenbenshæl, fik han øje på kvadrantens knuste kobbersigterør, som han havde smadret mod dækket dagen før.

»Du stakkels, stolte himmelgransker og solens lods! I går ødelagde jeg dig, og i dag ville kompasserne gerne have ødelagt mig. Så, så. Men Ahab er stadig herre over den vandrette magnetjernsten. Mr. Starbuck — en lanse uden skaft; en topmaul og den mindste af sejlmagerens nåle. Hurtigt!«

Måske bidrog nogle kloge motiver til drivkraften bag det, han nu stod i begreb med at gøre, motiver hvis formål kunne være at oplive besætningens mod med et mesterstykke af hans snilde i en sag så forunderlig som de omvendte kompasser. Desuden vidste den gamle mand godt, at det at styre efter omvendte nåle, om end klodset muligt, ikke var noget, overtroiske sømænd lod passere uden gysen og anelser om ondt.

»Mænd,« sagde han og vendte sig roligt mod besætningen, mens styrmanden rakte ham tingene, han havde bedt om, »mine mænd, tordenen har vendt gamle Ahabs nåle om; men af dette stykke stål kan Ahab lave en af sine egne, der peger lige så rigtigt som nogen.«
Mens han sagde det, udvekslede sømændene undselige blikke af slavisk undren og ventede med fascinerede øjne på, hvilken magi der nu ville komme. Men Starbuck så væk.

Med et slag af topmaulen slog Ahab lansens stålhoved af, rakte så styrmanden den lange jernstang, der var tilbage, og bad ham holde den oprejst uden at lade den røre dækket. Så slog han gentagne gange på stangens øvre ende med maulen, satte den afstumpede nål på højkant oven på den og hamrede på den, mindre kraftigt, flere gange, mens styrmanden stadig holdt stangen som før. Så gik han i gang med nogle små, mærkelige bevægelser — om de var nødvendige for at magnetisere stålet eller blot skulle øge besætningens ærefrygt, er uvist — og bad om linnedtråd; og han gik hen til nathuset, tog de to omvendte nåle ud og hængte sejlnålen vandret i midten over et af kompaskortene. Først gik stålet rundt og rundt og dirrede og vibrerede i begge ender; men til sidst faldt det til ro på sin plads, og Ahab, der havde fulgt spændt med efter dette resultat, trådte åbent tilbage fra nathuset og pegede med udstrakt arm på det og udbrød: »Se selv efter, om ikke Ahab er herre over den vandrette magnetjernsten! Solen er i øst, og det kompas sværger på det!«
Én efter én kikkede de ind — for kun deres egne øjne kunne overbevise mænd så uvidende som dem — og én efter én listede de væk.
Så kunne man se Ahab i hele hans skæbnesvangre stolthed, i de brændende øjne fulde af foragt og triumf.
